newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Court rejects parts of S.Africa's new constitution.
newsitem.headline: Court rejects parts of S.Africa's new constitution.

text.p: South Africa's most powerful court on Friday rejected parts of the country's post-apartheid constitution thrashed out in several years of talks which brought the country to democracy.
But the court ruled that flaws in the document could be fixed quite easily by the political negotiators who had settled on several uncomfortable compromises in smoke-filled rooms.
Constitutional Court approval is essential before the 140-page document can become law, but the court's 11 judges said they were not satisfied with some of its provisions.

"We are unable to and therefore do not certify that all of the provisions of the Constitution of the Republic of South Africa 1996 comply with the constitutional principles," court President Arthur Chaskalson said in the judgment.

"We wish to conclude this judgment with two observations. The first is to reiterate that the Constitutional Assembly has drafted a constitutional text which complies with the overwhelming majority of the requirements of the constitutional principles.

"The second is that the instances of non-compliance, although singly and collectively important, should present no significant obstacle to the formulation of a text which complies fully with those requirements," Chaskalson said.
The 490-member Constitutional Assembly approved the constitution in May after months of wrangling over labour rights and provincial government powers.

Analysts said the court decision meant the document would have to go back to the leaders of the Constitutional Assembly to decide on the way forward, as the new constitution does include explicit provisions on a procedure to be followed after the rebuffal.

The constitution, which was intended to replace a two-year old transitional one, was to be phased in over several years to 1999, when new elections are to be held for the first majority rule government that is not part of an enforced coalition.

President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress rules in an uneasy unity government with the Inkatha Freedom Party, after the white-led National Party pulled out of the cabinet to go into opposition at the end of June.
